citations.quote: Let $X$ be a compact connected oriented topological $4$-manifold with nonempty boundary, let $x_0\in X$, and put $G=\pi_1(X,x_0)$. A **finite relative disk-embedding datum** consists of proper generic immersions $f_i:(D^2,S^1)\looparrowright(X,\partial X)$, $1\le i\le n$, whose boundary circles are embedded and pairwise disjoint, together with framed immersed spheres $g_i:S^2\looparrowright\operatorname{int}X$ that are algebraically dual to the disks. Here a generic immersion is locally a topological embedding except at finitely many double points, each with exactly two preimages whose image sheets are the coordinate planes $\mathbb R^2\times\{0\}$ and $\{0\}\times\mathbb R^2$ in a chart of $X$; proper means that the inverse image of $\partial X$ is exactly the domain boundary; and framed means that the normal microbundle has a chosen trivialization extending the specified boundary framing. Choose paths from $x_0$ to the immersed surfaces and orient the surfaces. Each transverse intersection $p$ of two surfaces contributes $\epsilon(p)g_p$ to $\lambda$, where $\epsilon(p)\in\{1,-1\}$ compares their induced local orientation with the chosen orientation of $X$, and $g_p\in G$ is the loop that travels along the chosen path to the first surface, then to $p$, and returns along the second surface and its chosen path. Thus $\lambda$ is a signed equivariant intersection sum in $\mathbb Z[G]$. Wall's self-intersection sum $\mu$ is the signed sum over self-double points in $\mathbb Z[G]/\langle g-g^{-1}:g\in G\rangle$, because interchanging the two sheets replaces a label by its inverse. The normal framing is a separate datum; its relative normal Euler or boundary-framing obstruction is zero precisely when the specified framing extends over the immersion. The spheres are **algebraically dual** when $\lambda(f_i,g_j)=\delta_{ij}$, $\lambda(g_i,g_j)=0$ for every $i,j$, and $\mu(g_i)=0$ for every $i$. The disk data are **algebraically unobstructed** when also $\lambda(f_i,f_j)=0$ for $i\ne j$ and $\mu(f_i)=0$ for every $i$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

citations.quote: Let $\Gamma$ be a group. Say that $\Gamma$ is **good for the Freedman disk-embedding theorem** when it has the $\pi_1$-null disk property: for every disk-like capped grope $G^c$ of height $1.5$ with a chosen basepoint and every homomorphism $\phi:\pi_1(G^c)\to\Gamma$, there is an immersed disk whose framed boundary is the attaching region of $G^c$, such that each double-point loop of the disk, regarded after basing as an element of $\pi_1(G^c)$, is sent to the identity by $\phi$. This definition of a good group is a hypothesis on $\Gamma$; it does not assert that any particular group is good.

> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K:S^1\hookrightarrow S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere, and let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, oriented so that its boundary orientation is the given orientation of $K$. Let $g$ be the nonnegative integer determined by $\chi(F)=1-2g$. Choose an ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of the first singular homology group $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$, represented by integral one-cycles on $F$. Orient the normal line of $F$ by requiring $(n,u,v)$ to be positively oriented in $S^3$ whenever $(u,v)$ is a positive tangent basis of $F$. The positive push-off $a_i^+$ is the cycle carried to a sufficiently small positive normal level in a bicollar of $F$.

For disjoint oriented closed curves $J,L\subset S^3$, orient a meridian $\mu_L$ of $L$ so that a positive tangent to $L$ followed by a positive basis of its normal disk gives the ambient orientation. The linking number $\operatorname{lk}(J,L)$ is the integer determined by $[J]=\operatorname{lk}(J,L)[\mu_L]$ in $H_1(S^3\setminus L;\mathbb Z)$, using the Alexander-duality identification that sends $[\mu_L]$ to $1$. Extend linking additively over integral one-cycles. The Seifert pairing is $\theta_F(x,y)=\operatorname{lk}(x^+,y)$, and its matrix in the chosen basis is $V=(V_{ij})_{i,j=1}^{2g}$, where $V_{ij}=\theta_F(a_i,a_j)=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. The surface and basis are part of the data; this definition asserts no knot-only matrix invariant.

Fix the orientation-reversing reflection $r:S^3\to S^3$ chosen for the mirror convention in the oriented connected-sum definition. If $K$ is a smooth oriented knot, its mirror $r(K)$ carries the orientation induced from $K$ by $r$. The reverse mirror of $K$, denoted $K^\dagger$, is the image $r(K)$ with its knot orientation reversed. Thus $K^\dagger$ changes both the ambient orientation convention and the orientation of the knot.

derivations.claim: For disjoint oriented curves $C,D\subset S^3$, choose oriented $2$-chains $A,B$ with $\partial A=C$ and $\partial B=D$, and perturb them to be transverse. The oriented intersection $1$-chain $A\cap B$ has boundary $(\partial A)\cap B-A\cap(\partial B)$, whose total signed boundary count is zero. Hence the signed intersection definitions give $\operatorname{lk}(C,D)=\operatorname{lk}(D,C)$.

In a bicollar of $F$, move the pair $(a_i^-,a_j)$ simultaneously in the positive normal direction by one collar width. The two curves remain on distinct normal levels, so this is an isotopy through disjoint pairs from $(a_i^-,a_j)$ to $(a_i,a_j^+)$. Linking is invariant under this isotopy, and by step 1.1 it is symmetric; therefore $\operatorname{lk}(a_i^-,a_j)=\operatorname{lk}(a_j^+,a_i)=V_{ji}$.

Reflection reverses the sign of linking. Because it reverses the ambient orientation, the image of the positive normal to $F$ is the negative normal to the reflected surface. Reversing the surface orientation afterward changes both tangent signs and leaves its positive normal unchanged. Thus the $(i,j)$ entry for the reverse mirror is $-\operatorname{lk}(a_i^-,a_j)=-V_{ji}$ by step 1.2. This holds for every $i,j$, so the matrix is $-V^T$.
The argument includes the empty basis: for $g=0$, both matrices are the unique $0\times0$ matrix and $-V^T=V$. This proves the stated identity in every genus.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, and let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface whose oriented boundary is $K$, with $\chi(F)=1-2g$. Choose an ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ and use the positive normal convention $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. Let $A_K$ be the first homology of the infinite cyclic cover of $S^3\setminus K$ classified by total linking, with $t$ acting by the positive-meridian deck transformation. Let $\Delta_K(t)$ be the generator of the zeroth elementary ideal $E_0(A_K)$ in $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$, and write $p\doteq q$ when $p$ and $q$ differ by a unit $\pm t^k$ of $\Lambda$. Then for every such $F$ and basis,

$$\det(V-tV^T)\doteq\Delta_K(t).$$

The determinant is $1$ for the empty $0\times0$ matrix when $g=0$. This formula concerns the polynomial $\Delta_K$; the existing knot-normalized fraction $D_K=\Delta_K/(1-t)$ is a separate invariant.

Let $V$ be an integral Seifert matrix in the positive-push convention $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. Two integral Seifert forms are **S-equivalent** when they are related by a finite sequence of integral unimodular basis changes and algebraic tube additions or their inverses. A basis change replaces $V$ by $P^T V P$ for $P\in\operatorname{GL}_m(\mathbb Z)$. A tube addition replaces $V$ by
$$
\begin{pmatrix}
V&0&\rho\\
0&0&1\\
\rho^T&0&0
\end{pmatrix},\qquad \rho\in\mathbb Z^m,
$$
where the two new basis elements are the short and long curves of the added tube. The **empty Seifert form** is the unique bilinear form on the zero module, represented by the $0\times0$ matrix.

derivations.claim: By [F1] and $\Delta_K(t)\doteq1$, the determinant $\det(V-tV^T)$ is a Laurent unit in $\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$. This verifies the Alexander-one hypothesis in the matrix convention of [F2].

The determinant calculation alone does not exhibit a sequence of integral basis changes and tube reductions from $V$ to the empty form. The needed implication is the S-equivalence theorem of Trotter used in the proof of Garoufalidis–Teichner Lemma 4.2; its proof has not yet been read completely or reconstructed locally. The claim is therefore not proved in this draft.

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. A positive Hopf band is an oriented annulus whose core has self-linking $+1$ in the positive-push convention. Let $F$ be the genus-one Seifert surface obtained by plumbing two positive Hopf bands in a square, with oriented core curves $a,b$ forming a positive handle basis, and choose the plumbing side so that $a^+$ bounds a disk in $S^3$ disjoint from $b$. The oriented boundary of this standard positive two-band plumbing is the right-handed trefoil. In the positive-push convention $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$ with ordered basis $(a,b)$, the Seifert matrix is
$$
V=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K:S^1\hookrightarrow S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere, and let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, oriented so that its boundary orientation is the given orientation of $K$. Let $g$ be the nonnegative integer determined by $\chi(F)=1-2g$. Choose an ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of the first singular homology group $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$, represented by integral one-cycles on $F$. Orient the normal line of $F$ by requiring $(n,u,v)$ to be positively oriented in $S^3$ whenever $(u,v)$ is a positive tangent basis of $F$. The positive push-off $a_i^+$ is the cycle carried to a sufficiently small positive normal level in a bicollar of $F$.

For disjoint oriented closed curves $J,L\subset S^3$, orient a meridian $\mu_L$ of $L$ so that a positive tangent to $L$ followed by a positive basis of its normal disk gives the ambient orientation. The linking number $\operatorname{lk}(J,L)$ is the integer determined by $[J]=\operatorname{lk}(J,L)[\mu_L]$ in $H_1(S^3\setminus L;\mathbb Z)$, using the Alexander-duality identification that sends $[\mu_L]$ to $1$. Extend linking additively over integral one-cycles. The Seifert pairing is $\theta_F(x,y)=\operatorname{lk}(x^+,y)$, and its matrix in the chosen basis is $V=(V_{ij})_{i,j=1}^{2g}$, where $V_{ij}=\theta_F(a_i,a_j)=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. The surface and basis are part of the data; this definition asserts no knot-only matrix invariant.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot with a Seifert surface $F$ and ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$, using $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$ for the positive-push Seifert matrix. Let $K^\dagger$ be the reverse mirror defined by the fixed orientation-reversing reflection followed by reversal of the knot orientation, and use the image basis on the reflected surface. The Seifert matrix of $K^\dagger$ in that basis is $-V^T$.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, and let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface whose oriented boundary is $K$, with $\chi(F)=1-2g$. Choose an ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ and use the positive normal convention $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. Let $A_K$ be the first homology of the infinite cyclic cover of $S^3\setminus K$ classified by total linking, with $t$ acting by the positive-meridian deck transformation. Let $\Delta_K(t)$ be the generator of the zeroth elementary ideal $E_0(A_K)$ in $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$, and write $p\doteq q$ when $p$ and $q$ differ by a unit $\pm t^k$ of $\Lambda$. Then for every such $F$ and basis,

$$\det(V-tV^T)\doteq\Delta_K(t).$$

The determinant is $1$ for the empty $0\times0$ matrix when $g=0$. This formula concerns the polynomial $\Delta_K$; the existing knot-normalized fraction $D_K=\Delta_K/(1-t)$ is a separate invariant.

Fix a coordinate orientation-reversing reflection $r:S^3\to S^3$ for the mirror convention. Let $K$ and $J$ be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere. A connected-sum datum consists of one smoothly embedded closed three-ball around a short subarc of $K$ and one around a short subarc of $J$, each meeting its knot in a single trivial properly embedded arc, together with the fixed standard orientation-reversing boundary identification of the two standard oriented ball boundaries that joins the oriented arcs into one circle. Choose this standard map once in the standard two-ball model so that it commutes with $r$ and an orientation-preserving half-turn interchanging the two balls preserves the joining convention. Here a trivial arc is an embedded interval in a ball that is carried by an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of ball-arc pairs to a straight diameter. Remove the interiors of the two balls and glue the remaining boundary spheres using this fixed identification; the resulting oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere is a connected sum of $K$ and $J$, denoted $K\#J$ for the specified datum.

The **standard unknot** is the oriented unit circle in a fixed coordinate two-plane of $S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$. A knot is **nontrivial** if it is not ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of $S^3$ to the standard unknot. A nontrivial knot is **prime** if it has no connected-sum presentation whose two summand knots are both nontrivial.

Let $X$ be a four-dimensional manifold with boundary and let $W$ be a compact surface with boundary. An embedding $e:(W,\partial W)\to(X,\partial X)$ is proper when $e^{-1}(\partial X)=\partial W$. It is locally flat at an interior point of $W$ when there are neighborhoods of the point and its image and a homeomorphism of pairs from those neighborhoods to $(\mathbb R^4,\mathbb R^2)$, with the standard linear plane $\mathbb R^2\subset\mathbb R^4$. It is locally flat at a boundary point when there are such neighborhoods and a homeomorphism of pairs to $(\mathbb R^4_+,\mathbb R^2_+)$, where $\mathbb R^4_+=\{x_4\geq0\}$ and $\mathbb R^2_+=\{x_2=x_3=0,\ x_4\geq0\}$; the line $\partial\mathbb R^2_+$ lies in $\partial\mathbb R^4_+$. derivations.claim: The right-handed trefoil matrix is $V=\begin{psmallmatrix}1&0\\-1&1\end{psmallmatrix}$ by [F1] in the convention [F2]. Choose the connected-sum balls around short boundary arcs where the Seifert surfaces are standard collars, disjoint from their basis curves and small positive push-offs. The fixed gluing [F5] joins those collars. A basis cycle in one summand and its push-off lie in a ball disjoint from the other summand's curves, so the first cycle bounds a $2$-chain there away from the second; hence all cross linking entries vanish. The combined matrix is therefore $W=\operatorname{diag}(V,-V^T)$ by [F3].

Direct calculation gives $\det(V-tV^T)=\det\begin{psmallmatrix}1-t&t\\-1&1-t\end{psmallmatrix}=(1-t)^2+t=t^2-t+1$. For the reverse-mirror block, $-V^T-t(-V)=tV-V^T$, whose determinant equals $\det(V-tV^T)$: transpose $tV-V^T$, then factor $-1$ from each of its two rows. Since $W-tW^T$ is block diagonal, its determinant is $(t^2-t+1)^2$. By [F2] and [F4], this is a representative of $\Delta_S(t)$.

Expanding $(t^2-t+1)^2$ gives $t^4-2t^3+3t^2-2t+1$, which has nonzero coefficients in degrees $0$ and $1$ and is therefore not a monomial $\pm t^k$. Since these monomials are exactly the units of $\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$, the Alexander polynomial is nonunit. On the other hand, [A2] supplies AC$_\omega$ from full AC, so [F7] gives a smooth ribbon disk; by [F8] this disk is locally flat. Thus $S$ is topologically slice despite its nonunit Alexander polynomial, refuting the asserted converse. For $T$, the same calculation gives $\Delta_T=t^2-t+1\not\doteq1$, which only means that the Alexander-one theorem does not apply.
